exercises.prompt: A Kotlin method is declared `@JvmOverloads fun send(to: String, subject: String = "", urgent: Boolean = false)`. How many `send` methods does a Java caller see?

feedback.message: Not yet — that would be without @JvmOverloads. The annotation adds overloads for the defaults.
Not yet — `to` has no default, so every overload must include it.

hints: One overload for each number of trailing defaults left out: none, one, or both.
exercises.solution: `@JvmOverloads` generates `send(String)`, `send(String, String)` and `send(String, String, boolean)`: **3** methods, just as the lesson's `deposit` produced three. Parameters with defaults can only be dropped from the end.

exercises.prompt: A file `Utils.kt` contains only top-level functions. What is the name of the class that Java code uses to call them (assuming no `@file:JvmName`)?

feedback.message: Nearly — the compiler adds a suffix to the file name.

exercises.solution: Top-level declarations in `Utils.kt` are compiled into static members of **`UtilsKt`**. Compiling such a file produces `UtilsKt.class`. Add `@file:JvmName("Utils")` at the top of the file to choose a nicer name for Java callers.

exercises.prompt: In the lesson's `Account`, `withBonus` is a companion-object function **without** `@JvmStatic`. How does Java code call it?

options.label: `Account.Companion.withBonus("Bao")`
options.feedback: Yes. Java reaches the companion instance through the static field `Companion`.

options.label: `Account.withBonus("Bao")`
options.feedback: Not yet — that works only for members annotated @JvmStatic, such as `open`.

options.label: `new Account().withBonus("Bao")`
options.feedback: Not yet — companion members do not belong to Account instances (and Account has no no-argument constructor).

hints: Look at the reflection output: where does `withBonus` appear?
exercises.solution: **a**. The reflection output listed `withBonus` only on `Account$Companion`, and `Account` has a static field `Companion` holding the instance. With `@JvmStatic`, as for `open`, the compiler also emits a static method on `Account` itself.

exercises.prompt: Using the lesson's `slugify`, what does `println(slugify("C# & Kotlin 2.4"))` print?

feedback.message: Not yet — `#` and `.` are not in `[a-z0-9]`, so they are replaced too.
Not yet — the dot between 2 and 4 is also a run of characters outside `[a-z0-9]`.

hints: Every run of characters outside a–z and 0–9 becomes one hyphen; then hyphens at the ends are trimmed.
exercises.solution: Lowercased, the title is `c# & kotlin 2.4`. The runs `# & `, ` ` and `.` are each replaced by one hyphen, giving `c-kotlin-2-4`, with nothing to trim: **`c-kotlin-2-4`**.

exercises.prompt: A Java method `String findNickname(String user)` has no nullability annotations and returns null for unknown users. Which Kotlin line is the safest way to use it?

options.label: `val nick: String = repo.findNickname(user) ?: user`
options.feedback: Yes. Treating the platform type as nullable and supplying a fallback handles the null case explicitly.

options.label: `val nick: String = repo.findNickname(user)`
options.feedback: Not yet — it compiles, but for an unknown user it throws a NullPointerException at this line.

options.label: `val nick = repo.findNickname(user)!!.trim()`
options.feedback: Not yet — `!!` turns the known null case into a crash.

hints: The documentation says the method can return null. How should Kotlin code treat a value that may be missing?
exercises.solution: **a**. A platform type can be treated as nullable or not; when the Java method can return null, treat it as nullable and handle it, here with an Elvis fallback. Annotating the Java method with `@Nullable` (from JSpecify, for example) would make Kotlin enforce this automatically.

exercises.prompt: A Kotlin function `fun load(path: String): String` can throw `java.io.IOException`. A Java caller writes `try { load(p); } catch (IOException e) { ... }` and javac reports an error. Why, and what fixes it?

options.label: Java forbids catching a checked exception that the called method does not declare; annotate the Kotlin function with `@Throws(IOException::class)`
options.feedback: Yes. Kotlin does not declare checked exceptions, so Java thinks load cannot throw IOException.

options.label: Kotlin functions cannot throw IOException; it must be wrapped in a RuntimeException
options.feedback: Not yet — Kotlin functions can throw any exception; the issue is only how the method is declared to Java.

options.label: Java must catch `kotlin.Exception` instead
options.feedback: Not yet — Kotlin's Exception is java.lang.Exception; the problem is the missing throws clause.

hints: What does the Java compiler check when it sees `catch (IOException e)` around a call?
exercises.solution: **a**. javac rejects a `catch` for a checked exception that nothing in the `try` block declares ("exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement"). Because Kotlin has no checked exceptions, its methods declare none unless you add `@Throws(IOException::class)`, which emits the Java `throws` clause.

exercises.prompt: In the mini test framework, `fun suite(name: String, block: TestSuite.() -> Unit)` lets the caller write `test("...") { ... }` inside the block without any prefix. Why?

options.label: `TestSuite.() -> Unit` is a function type with a receiver, so inside the lambda `this` is a TestSuite and its methods can be called directly
options.feedback: Yes. This is the mechanism behind Kotlin DSLs such as Gradle scripts and Kotest specs.

options.label: `test` is a global function defined by the standard library
options.feedback: Not yet — `test` is a method of TestSuite in this program.

options.label: `suite` copies the lambda's code into the TestSuite class at compile time
options.feedback: Not yet — nothing is copied into the class; the lambda is simply called with a TestSuite as its receiver (via `apply`).

hints: What does `TestSuite.()` in front of `-> Unit` mean?
exercises.solution: **a**. A lambda of type `TestSuite.() -> Unit` is called on a `TestSuite` receiver (here by `apply(block)`), so inside it `this` refers to that suite and `test(...)` means `this.test(...)`. The same idea makes `dependencies { implementation(...) }` work in a Gradle script.
